title: Illness as expiation
hook: no tiredness, illness or worry touches a believer, not even a thorn's prick, without wiping away some sins

segments.voice: Yesterday, 'iyadah, visiting the sick, and your line: the garden's harvest. Did you make the visit or the call? Today, the same bedside, seen from the bed. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

A thorn. Small enough to pull out with your fingernails, sharp enough to make you say ow. It's in a hadith, kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, and it's the smallest thing on a list. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, names what can happen to a believer: tiredness, illness, worry, sorrow, harm, distress. And then he goes all the way down, to the prick of a thorn. Even that, he says, is not for nothing. Today is about why.
screen: `A THORN.` → `THE SMALLEST THING ON THE LIST.` → `EVEN THAT, NOT FOR NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the hadith, in paraphrase. No tiredness, no illness, no worry, no sorrow, no harm and no distress befalls a Muslim, even the prick of a thorn, without Allah wiping away some of his sins by it. The word for that is kaffarah, expiation. In this picture, the hard hours of being sick are not empty hours. Something is happening in them, even when the person lying there can do nothing at all. Al-Bukhari keeps a story that shows how this was lived. Ibn 'Abbas once pointed out a woman to a student and said: shall I show you a woman of the people of Paradise? She had come to the Prophet with an illness that made her fall in fits, and asked him to pray for her cure. He gave her a choice. If you wish, be patient, and you will have Paradise. Or if you wish, I will pray to Allah to heal you. She chose patience. But she asked for one thing: that when the fits came, she wouldn't be uncovered. And he prayed for that. Now the other side, so the picture isn't bent. Patience here doesn't mean refusing a doctor. A hadith in Abu Dawud says, in paraphrase, that Allah sent down both disease and its remedy, so seek treatment. The medicine and the patience aren't rivals. You take the pills. You wait for the results. And the waiting, in this hadith, counts too.
screen: `EVEN THE PRICK OF A THORN.` · `KAFFARAH: EXPIATION.` · `THE WOMAN WHO CHOSE PATIENCE.` · `SEEK THE REMEDY TOO.`

segments.voice: The practice: bear an illness patiently. Settle, and breathe. Scan your body slowly, from your head down to your feet. Where is something tired, aching, or not quite right? It may be small: a stiff neck, a tired back, a worry sitting in your chest. Don't fight it, and don't push it away. Just let your attention rest on it, and breathe around it. If nothing hurts today, think of someone for whom something does. If you pray, you can hold that ache up as it is, and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Illness as expiation. In the hadith, even a thorn's prick wipes away some sins; the hard hours are not empty. Today's word.
Your line: nothing is wasted. The next time something small hurts or worries you today, notice it, and let the line come back. Tomorrow, remembering death. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims who are ill often recall the hadith that illness and even a thorn's prick wipe away sins, and pair patience with seeking medical treatment, which the hadith also encourage.

fork.setup: you're ill, and the Prophet offers you a choice: be patient and have Paradise, or he'll pray for your cure. what do you choose?
options: patience, but ask not to be uncovered.
fork.reveal: in al-Bukhari, the woman chose patience and asked only not to be uncovered during her fits, and he prayed for that.

original.note: Arabic: expiation, the wiping away of sins.

trapdoor: what you thought: illness is just bad luck to get through.
what it means: in the hadith, every hardship, down to a thorn's prick, wipes away some sins; the hours of illness are not empty.
what a scholar hears: the list in al-Bukhari from tiredness to the thorn, the woman of Paradise who chose patience, and the remedy hadith beside them.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5641–5642 (no tiredness, illness, worry … not even a thorn's prick, but Allah expiates sins by it)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5652 (Ibn 'Abbas: the woman with fits who chose patience)
Sunan Abi Dawud 3874 (Allah sent down the disease and the remedy; seek treatment)
